title: The Northern Tribes: Warriors, Grief, and a Builder
summary: The chapter gathers the genealogies of the northern tribes: Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher, most of them counted by their fighting men. Two passages stand out: the grief of Ephraim over sons killed in a raid and the naming of a new son for that tragedy, and the line from Ephraim to Joshua son of Nun. Sheerah, a daughter of Ephraim's house, is remembered for building towns.
story: With Judah, Simeon, the eastern tribes, and Levi behind him, the Chronicler now covers the tribes of the north, the heartland of the kingdom that broke away from David's house after Solomon and fell to Assyria in 722 BC. By his day these tribes had been scattered for centuries. Yet he lists them, because his Israel is all twelve tribes, not only the survivors in Judah. The entries are short, often shaped like military rolls, and some tribes receive only a verse. Still, each one is named and counted. In the middle of the lists, the story of Ephraim's grief breaks through, and at its end stands Joshua, who led Israel into the land. The chapter sets up chapter 8, which returns to Benjamin in full, the tribe of Saul.
historical:
Several entries count mighty men of valor recorded in genealogies, and verse 2 dates one census to the days of David. The numbers may come from military registers of the united monarchy, perhaps connected with David's census (chapter 21) or his army organization (chapter 27). Issachar's land lay in the Jezreel Valley in the north; Naphtali lived west of the Sea of Galilee; Asher lay along the coast north of Mount Carmel. Ephraim and Manasseh, the Joseph tribes, held the central hill country, and verses 28 and 29 name their chief towns: Bethel, Gezer, Shechem, and on Manasseh's side Beth-shean, Taanach, Megiddo, and Dor. Those four were strong Canaanite cities that Manasseh at first failed to capture (Judges 1:27), and they became Israelite only later.

The list omits two tribes altogether: Dan and Zebulun. Scholars have proposed several reasons, including damage to the Chronicler's sources, a loss of text in copying, and the possibility that the Hushites of verse 12 represent Dan (Hushim is Dan's son in Genesis 46:23). None is certain. The Chronicler clearly knew both tribes, since he names them in 2:1-2 and in David's army (12:33 and 12:35).
cultural:
Most of this chapter reads like a muster roll, and that is probably what much of it was. In ancient Israel the heads of families were responsible for providing fighting men when the tribes were called out, and genealogical records doubled as military registers. To be a mighty man of valor was to be an able-bodied warrior of good standing; the same phrase could describe a man of substance in his community.

The Ephraim passage shows ancient mourning customs. When a father lost his sons, relatives came to sit with him and comfort him, sometimes for days (compare Job 2:11-13). Naming a child after the circumstances of the birth was common, and Beriah's name is explained by a Hebrew phrase meaning in tragedy or in disaster. The story also shows that raiding livestock was a normal hazard of life between neighboring peoples, and that it could end badly. Sheerah's building of Lower and Upper Beth-horon (verse 24) is unusual. Women in the ancient Near East rarely appear as builders of towns, and this brief line credits a woman with founding or fortifying an important pair of towns on the road from the coast into the hill country.
literary: The chapter strings together tribal entries of different lengths and formats. Issachar and Benjamin (verses 1 to 12) have military totals. Naphtali has a single verse. Manasseh (verses 14 to 19) is tangled and hard to follow in Hebrew, with women prominent: an Aramean concubine, Maacah, Hammolecheth, and Zelophehad's daughters. Ephraim's section (verses 20 to 29) contains the one narrative in the chapter, told in a few sentences with real feeling: sons killed, a father mourning, relatives comforting, a new child named for sorrow. It then ends with a linear list down to Joshua, which gives Ephraim's story a hopeful close. Asher (verses 30 to 40) returns to the military form and ends on a total of fighting men.

outline.t: Ephraim: grief, a builder, Joshua, and their towns

doctrines.note: Ephraim's grief is recorded without explanation or rebuke. He mourned for many days, his family comforted him, and life continued with the birth of another child. Scripture gives room for real sorrow among God's people.
From a household marked by tragedy came Joshua, who would lead Israel into the land. The chapter quietly shows God working through a grieving family to raise up a leader.
The Chronicler lists tribes that had long since been scattered, because they still belonged to the people of God. His picture of Israel refuses to forget members who were lost.

words.note: Gibbor, a mighty man or warrior. Combined with chayil (strength or valor), it forms the phrase mighty men of valor that recurs through the chapter. The same word describes God as a mighty warrior elsewhere, and in chapter 11 it will name David's elite fighters.

Eleph, usually thousand, used for the large totals in this chapter. The same word can also mean a clan or a military unit, and some scholars think certain totals originally counted units rather than individual men. Either way, the numbers present the tribes as organized and ready for service.

Nacham, to comfort or to be sorry (verse 22). Ephraim's relatives came to comfort him. The word is used later of God comforting his people after exile, as in Isaiah 40:1, and here it shows family solidarity in grief.

Banah, to build. Sheerah built Lower and Upper Beth-horon. Building is a theme the Chronicler cares about, since the book moves toward David's plans and Solomon's building of the temple, and here a woman of Ephraim is remembered as a builder.

christ: The chapter's high point is the line from Ephraim to Joshua son of Nun (verses 25 to 27). Joshua led Israel across the Jordan into the promised land. His name in Hebrew, Yehoshua, means the LORD saves, and its later forms, Yeshua in Hebrew and Iesous in Greek, give us the name Jesus. The letter to the Hebrews contrasts the two: Joshua gave Israel the land, but not the final rest God promised, which still remains for God's people and is entered through faith (Hebrews 4:8-10). The connection is a pattern the New Testament itself draws, not a prediction in the genealogy. The chapter's grief-to-hope movement in Ephraim's family also fits the wider story the Bible tells, though it is not a prophecy of Christ.

hard.q: Why are the tribes of Dan and Zebulun missing from the genealogies?
hard.a: Chapters 2 to 8 cover every tribe except Dan and Zebulun. Several explanations have been offered. Some think the Chronicler's sources for those tribes were lost or unavailable. Others suggest a copying error removed material, perhaps in or near verse 12, where the Hushites may originally have belonged to Dan (Genesis 46:23 names Hushim as Dan's son). A few have argued that Dan was omitted because of its early idolatry (Judges 18), but Zebulun has no such story, and the Chronicler includes Dan in David's army (12:35), which weakens that view. The honest answer is that the reason is uncertain. What is clear is that the Chronicler's picture of Israel includes all twelve tribes, as his opening list in 2:1-2 and his list of David's supporters in chapter 12 show.

questions: Ephraim mourned for many days, and his relatives came to comfort him. How do you respond to grief in others, and how have you been comforted in your own?
From a family marked by loss came Joshua, who led Israel into the land. Where have you seen good come out of a household's sorrow?
The Chronicler lists tribes long scattered, refusing to forget them. Who in your church or family has drifted away but still belongs, and how might you remember them?
